segments.en: Hear that? Talking drums, horns from yellow buses, a radio playing Afrobeats and someone laughing loudly at a joke. That is the soundtrack of a Nigerian street, and it is full of life.

Nigeria has more people than any other country in Africa, and more than two hundred and fifty ethnic groups. The three largest are the Hausa in the north, the Yoruba in the southwest and the Igbo in the southeast.
Hundreds of languages are spoken here. English is the official one, and Nigerian Pidgin lets people from every corner chat together. How far? is a friendly way to ask how you are doing.
Respect for elders runs deep. A Yoruba child may kneel or bow to greet an older relative, and you will often hear people called Auntie or Uncle even when they are not family at all.
Lagos, on the Atlantic coast, is a giant city of markets, music studios, bridges and lagoons. Abuja, the capital, was built in the centre of the country, beneath the great granite dome of Aso Rock.
Head north and the land dries into savanna. The ancient city of Kano has dye pits where cloth has been soaked in deep blue indigo for centuries.
Now, food. Jollof rice, cooked in a rich tomato and pepper sauce, is served at every party, and Nigerians will happily tell you theirs is the best in West Africa.
There is also pounded yam with egusi soup, spicy grilled meat called suya sold at night by the roadside, and sweet fried plantain called dodo.
Clothes are a celebration too. At weddings, whole families wear matching fabric called aso ebi, and the women tie tall, beautifully folded headwraps called gele.
Nigeria is a powerhouse of creativity. Its film industry, Nollywood, makes a huge number of movies every year, and Afrobeats artists fill stadiums around the world.
The written word matters too. Chinua Achebe wrote the novel Things Fall Apart, and Wole Soyinka became the first African to win the Nobel Prize for Literature.
Festivals light up the calendar. At the Durbar in the north, horsemen in brilliant robes charge past the emir, and at the Osun festival, crowds walk to a sacred river grove in Osogbo.
Before you go, share a plate of jollof and dance a little when the music starts. Then cross the border west into Benin, where the story of the Yoruba and their neighbours continues.
